prompt.context: Our client is a large telecom service provider. In the past the telecom industry has enjoyed a monopoly as various regional telecom companies established monopolies under government protection. Recently the US government has passed a new law that allows competitors to enter other regional areas where there is already an incumbent present. The competitor (new entrant) can lease the incumbent's infrastructure and target the incumbent's customers. The incumbent will HAVE to charge the price set by the government. The client has seen some cannibalization in their region, so they set up a new division to penetrate other regions. However, for the last 2 years that venture/division has been unprofitable.
prompt.question: The CEO wants your judgment before he makes a decision to shut the division down. Should the client shut down this new division?

clarifying_info.q: How many customers has the new group signed up?
What is the price charged per customer?
clarifying_info.a: The average price per customer per month is $38.60, which is 10% less than the competition (incumbent)

SG&A is $5.10 per customer per month — half is fixed cost and half is variable cost. The government has set a price of $36.90 per customer per month that the client must pay to the incumbent for leasing infrastructure.
The client believes they can reduce SG&A by 10% at most without affecting quality of business.

clarifying_info.q: Are all customers paying the same price?
clarifying_info.a: There is some price discrimination. 90% of customers are non-business (residential) consumers and 10% are business consumers. Business customers pay higher prices than non-business customers.

framework: Understand the revenue structure: number of customers, pricing, customer segments
Analyze the cost structure: variable costs (government-mandated infrastructure lease), SG&A (fixed vs. variable split)
Calculate per-customer profitability and assess break-even feasibility
Evaluate whether costs can be reduced or revenue can be increased
Assess customer mix and strategic options (segment shift, pricing strategy)
Formulate recommendation: shut down, restructure, or pivot strategy

questions.prompt: Is the division profitable on a per-customer basis? Calculate the per-customer monthly profit/loss.
questions.guidance: A strong answer immediately identifies that revenue minus total cost yields a loss. Candidate should note that even before considering fixed costs, the variable cost alone (government price + variable SG&A) may exceed revenue. Key insight: the government-mandated price of $36.90 is non-negotiable, so the candidate should focus on whether the remaining cost components can be reduced enough to achieve profitability.

math.setup: Revenue per customer per month = $38.60. Total cost per customer per month = government lease price + SG&A = $36.90 + $5.10 = $42.00. Profit per customer per month = Revenue - Total Cost.
steps: Variable cost check: govt price ($36.90) + variable SG&A ($5.10 x 50% = $2.55) = $39.45. Even at variable cost level, revenue of $38.60 < variable cost of $39.45, so the division loses money even before fixed costs.
If SG&A is reduced by 10%: new SG&A = $5.10 x 0.90 = $4.59. New total cost = $36.90 + $4.59 = $41.49. New profit = $38.60 - $41.49 = -$2.89 per customer. Still unprofitable.
Annual loss at 1MM customers: $3.40 x 12 x 1,000,000 = $40.8 million per year
math.answer: The division loses $3.40 per customer per month. Even with maximum 10% SG&A reduction, it still loses $2.89 per customer per month. The division is unprofitable at a variable cost level, making it structurally unsound under the current pricing/customer mix.

questions.prompt: Why is the client charging 10% less than the incumbent, and is this justified?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this as an aggressive market penetration pricing strategy to gain customers in a new region. The client is sacrificing margin to build market share. A strong candidate will note this pricing is likely unsustainable given the already-negative margins.

questions.prompt: Given the customer mix (90% non-business, 10% business), what strategic options exist?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify that business customers are price-inelastic and willing to pay premium prices due to peak-load pricing dynamics and business necessity. The client is heavily weighted toward price-sensitive residential consumers, which creates margin pressure. The strategic recommendation should pivot toward targeting business consumers to achieve higher average revenue per customer.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors explain why the division is unprofitable, and what levers could improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue levers
ideas: Raise prices closer to or at incumbent levels (currently 10% discount is unsustainable)
Shift customer mix toward business consumers who accept higher prices
Introduce tiered service offerings with premium tiers
Cross-sell additional telecom services to existing 1MM customers

categories.name: Cost levers
ideas: Reduce SG&A (max 10% reduction per management estimate)
Achieve scale economies as customer base grows
Renegotiate government-set infrastructure lease price (if future policy change occurs)
Improve operational efficiency in the variable SG&A component

categories.name: Strategic options
ideas: Pivot new division to target business consumers exclusively
Exit the new region and focus on defending home region
Partner with another entrant to share infrastructure lease costs
Lobby for lower government-mandated lease rates

recommendation: Do not shut down the division yet — the client has successfully acquired 1 million customers in 2 years, demonstrating strong market penetration capability
Pivot the division's strategy from targeting price-sensitive non-business (residential) consumers to targeting business consumers, who are price-inelastic and willing to pay premium prices
This segment shift would allow the client to raise average revenue per customer above the $42.00 cost threshold and achieve profitability
risks: Business customers may already be locked into long-term contracts with the incumbent
Competing for business customers requires different sales capabilities and service levels
The transition period will require continued losses while the customer mix shifts
If unable to win business customers, the division may need to be shut down
next_steps: Quantify the price business customers pay vs. $38.60 average to confirm profitability potential
Assess the size of the addressable business customer market in target regions
Develop a sales strategy and timeline for transitioning the division's focus to business customers
Set a performance milestone (e.g., 6-12 months) to evaluate whether the pivot is working before revisiting the shutdown decision
